In the eighteenth century makers developed interchangeable crooks, so that a single instrument could be used in different keys. After that the valve system was the important change, altering pitch by adding length of tubing; the standard three-valve layout was almost universal by 1864 at the latest, as the Arban method bears witness. Natural brass continued in use afterwards for historical performance, ceremonial occasions, and modern scores by Richard Wagner, Richard Strauss and others.

Natural and keyed brass are mostly used for historical performance on Baroque and Classical instruments, and also appear in certain ceremonial settings; the modern scores of Wagner and Richard Strauss occasionally call for natural brass to obtain a particular intonation or timbre. A brass instrument is one that sounds when the player's lip vibration makes the air inside a tubular resonator resonate; it is Hornbostel–Sachs class 423. Its tube length can be changed by valves, a slide, crooks or keys, and the player then chooses an overtone with the embouchure, lip tension and airflow. Modern brass players mostly use valved instruments, including the trumpet, French horn, euphonium and tuba; the slide family is led by the trombone. Natural and keyed brass appear in historical performance of Baroque and Classical instruments, in certain ceremonies, and in some modern works.

The source points out that some instruments classed as brass are made of wood, such as the alphorn, the cornett, the serpent and the didgeridoo; others are made from animal horn, as the shofar is, from shell, as the conch is, and from plastic, as the vuvuzela is. 銅管樂器的音色來自吹奏者嘴唇振動與管內空氣共振；口型、嘴唇張力與氣流決定所選泛音: The timbre of a brass instrument comes from the player's lip vibration and the resonance of the air in the tube; the embouchure, lip tension and airflow determine which overtone is chosen, and the slide, valves, crooks or keys change the tube length and the overtone series. Cylindrical bores usually sound brighter and more penetrating, conical bores gentler. A whole-tube instrument has a relatively wide bore and can sound the fundamental more steadily; a half-tube instrument has a relatively narrow bore and its lowest practical note is usually the first overtone, so range and timbre vary with bore, tube length and the way the instrument is sounded.
